title: KCY v XSH
text:
NOTE: This determination
contains an order prohibiting
publication of the applicant’s
name and various other
information (see [3], [4] and [83]).
IN THE EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS AUTHORITY
AUCKLAND
I TE RATONGA AHUMANA TAIMAHI
TĀMAKI MAKAURAU ROHE
[2026] NZERA 516
3312180
BETWEEN KCY
Applicant
AND XSH
Respondent
Member of Authority: Peter Fuiava
Representatives: Mark Donovan, counsel for Applicant
Matthew McGoldrick, counsel for the Respondent
Investigation Meeting: 23-24 February 2026 in Auckland
Submissions and other 13 March, 23, 29 April, and 29 July 2026 from the
information received: Applicant
26 March, 24 April and 28 July 2026 from the
Respondent
Determination: 3 August 2026
DETERMINATION OF THE AUTHORITY
A non-publication order of the applicant’s name is granted
[1] The applicant, whose name has been depersonalised as KCY, applies for a
non-publication order of her name and any other details that might lead to her identity.
The primary basis for the application is that KCY is currently unemployed and is
actively seeking new employment. Her concern is the prejudicial impact publication
of her name would have on her future employment prospects. The respondent takes a
neutral position with respect to the application.

[2] The Employment Relations Act 2000 (the Act) affords the Authority the
discretion to make a non-publication order of the name of any party or witness subject
to such conditions as it thinks fit.1 The Employment Court has provided a two-step
process in assessing such applications; first, there must be a reason to believe that
specific adverse consequences could reasonably be expected to occur if publication
was allowed; second, consideration must then be given as to whether the adverse
consequences are significant enough to justify a departure from the principle of open
justice.2
[3] I was referred to FDE v UWV as authority of what her Honour Chief Judge
Inglis identified as a broader public interest in supporting, where appropriate, the
rights of individuals to privacy in order to access the labour market.3 However, in that
case, the applicant’s name had already been published in an Authority determination
and in a subsequent judgment on challenge from the Employment Court. While this
distinguishes that case to the present one, medical information has been provided to
the Authority showing that KCY has had a history of depression since September
2022 and was on antidepressant medication until recently.4 Although the cause of the
applicant’s mental health concerns is the subject of this determination, when
considered in combination with the inordinate period she has been out of work and
her desire to return to the workforce, I am satisfied that both limbs of Spiga are met so
as to displace the principle of open justice. Consequently, a permanent non-
publication order of the applicant’s name is granted pursuant to Sch 2 cl 10 of the Act.
[4] To ensure that she cannot be identified by deduction, particularly as her
ethnicity is front and centre of this determination, the respondent (XSH or the
company), its various retail stores, and its witnesses have all been depersonalised. By
consent, a non-publication order has also been granted concerning video footage and
third-party receipts that KCY provided to the Authority to support her case.
What is the employment relationship problem?
[5] In broad terms, KCY has requested that the Authority investigate claims of
unjustified disadvantage in the nature of alleged workplace bullying and racial
1 The Act, Sch 2, cl 10.
2 MW v Spiga [2024] NZEmpC 147, [2024] ERNZ 678 at [88]-[89].
3 FDE v UWV [2024] NZEmpC 179 at [25].
4 Common bundle of documents, 12 November 2025, p 355.

discrimination by her previous store manager. In addition, KCY says that she was
unjustifiably dismissed by XSH for serious misconduct in an apparent breach of its
Goods with Purchase (GWP) policy as well as a breach of confidential information
relating to a passcode to a secure back-office area that KCY gave to a member of staff
who the company says was not authorised to receive it.
How has the Authority investigated?
[6] For its investigation, KCY provided the Authority with two written witness
statements. For its case, XSH called five witnesses who have been referred to in this
determination by their job title only. Those witnesses comprised:
• the Head of HR;
• the regional HR manager;
• the store Regional Manager;
• the HR Manager Operations; and
• the manager of another XSH retail store in which the applicant did not
work.
[7] All witnesses answered questions under oath or affirmation from me and the
parties’ representatives. As permitted by s 174E of the Act, this determination has
stated findings of fact and law, expressed conclusions on issues necessary to dispose
of the matter and specified orders made. It has not recorded all evidence and
submissions received.
What are the issues?
[8] Following a case management conference with the representatives on
8 August 2025, the issues for investigation and determination are as follows:
(i) Was KCY unjustifiably dismissed?
(ii) Was she unjustifiably disadvantaged regarding complaints she made
in 2022 and 2023, concerning a transfer to another store, and in the
way she was suspended?
(iii) KCY seeks lost wages, compensation for hurt and humiliation under
s 123(1)(c)(i) of the Act, general damages and penalties.

(iv) If any of these remedies are awarded, should there be a reduction
under s 124 of the Act for contribution?
(v) Should either party contribute to the costs of representation of the
other?
What happened?
[9] KCY is of Russian ethnicity and English is her second language. She worked
for XSH from 7 October 2019 until her employment ended on 20 May 2024 for
serious misconduct. At the time of her dismissal, KCY was the beauty sales manager
of one of the company’s retail stores.
[10] On 20 November 2022, KCY sent the first of two emails to the regional HR
manager hoping to catch up with her any time the following week. There was no
reply to that email.
[11] Two days later, KCY sent a second email to the regional HR manager on
22 November stating that while she loved her job, she experienced “a certain attitude”
from her store manager which she personally classified as bullying and which caused
her a lot of discomfort. KCY further stated:
This is a serious allegation therefore I would like to hear a second opinion
from HR and advice on how to proceed further.
[12] The regional HR manager responded later that same afternoon apologising for
her late reply and indicated that she could meet with KCY in person later that week or
by video call the next day. KCY replied that she wished to meet later that week and
outside of work which would also give her time to put her statement and all her notes
together.
[13] On 29 November 2022, KCY and the regional HR manager met to discuss her
concerns about alleged bullying by the store manager. The regional HR manager’s
file note of that meeting records that KCY was upset and tearful and that she felt
bullied by her store manager who did not like Russians and who talked about the
Ukraine and Russia war while at work. Because KCY had family in that part of the

world and was upset by news of the conflict, she believed there was no need for the
store manager to speak about the war at work also.
[14] The applicant and the regional HR manager are in dispute as to what was to
happen next. According to the regional HR manager, KCY had made it clear to her at
the meeting that she did not want her to speak to the store manager and that she
wished her to keep their conversation confidential. She also understood that the
applicant wished to deal with matters informally and that she would talk to the store
manager on her own. However, the applicant says that she did not wish the regional
HR manager to approach the store manager that day and that it was her expectation
that HR would approach the store manager at some point to arrange potential
mediation between them.
[15] On 7 December 2022, the regional HR manager texted KCY to check in on her
and advised that she would be flying overseas but would be back later that month. If
there was anything that the applicant needed in the meantime, the regional HR
manager referred her to another HR staff member in her absence.
[16] There was no further response from KCY although she says that she texted the
regional HR manager to wish her a good holiday. However, evidence of that text was
not provided to the Authority. The regional HR manager stated that having heard
nothing further from the applicant, she assumed that the matter had resolved itself.
[17] Shortly after KCY’s first meeting with the regional HR manager on
29 November 2022, she had a private conversation with her store manager who
assured her that she would treat her with respect and professionalism. However, in
spite of that assurance, KCY stated that the store manager’s behaviour returned the
following year and that XSH had previously been put on notice of serious allegations
of bullying that were impacting her health which the company had failed to do
anything about.
[18] On 11 September 2023, some ten months after KCY’s first email to the
regional HR manager on 20 November 2022, she emailed the regional HR manager
stating:

Once again I am bringing to your attention that I have been bullied and
harassed at work because of my nationality by [the store manager] since I’ve
started to work at [XSH].
You saw me being very upset and as I told you my story I couldn’t stop
crying. You said that if I wanted to go further and make an official
complaint there would be an investigation, I said that I was very emotionally
drained and going into Christmas I didn’t have strength and spear [sic]
energy to go through additional stress.
Instead I had a meeting with sm (store manager) later that week and I told her
again that I would like her not to talk negative about my nationality and
about war at work, I explained to her AGAIN that I had family in Ukraine
and Russia and being exposed to this subject at work making me feel VERY
bad and anxious. She replied that she was “obsessed about war”.
[19] The applicant’s email explained that the store manager had stopped reading
news about Russia from social media on her phone during management meetings for a
little while but that lately it had started to escalate. KCY went on to explain that on
6 September 2023, before going to work, she started to experience a panic attack. She
expressed that she did not want to go the office all that day fearing that she would be
approached by her store manager and have another anxiety attack. KCY alleged that
the store manager personally disliked Russians and was constantly targeting her.
[20] On 13 September 2023, the regional HR manager met with KCY for a second
time at a nearby store outside of her place of work. The regional HR manager’s file
note of that meeting records that KCY was upset and crying and that she had said that
she was unwell and was anxious. She advised that after approaching the store
manager in November 2022, the store manager had stopped talking about the
Russia/Ukraine war for a while but in the last three months had started up again.
[21] The following day, the regional HR manager accompanied by the store
Regional Manager, went to the store in which the applicant worked to speak to the
store manager as KCY had given her consent for them to address her concerns
immediately. According to a file note by the regional HR manager, the store manager
had denied watching videos of the Ukraine/Russia conflict on the shop floor or in
front of KCY and that while she was interested in the war, she did not intend to hurt
her. The store Regional Manager is recorded as having said to the store manager:
You could have a grievance if you don’t stop. She perceives you to be
talking to others about your political views …

You owe her an apology …
You need to stay private and don’t share or talk to anyone moving forward
about Russia or the war.
[22] At a follow-up meeting between KCY and the regional HR manager on
20 September 2023, KCY requested a formal investigation and for disciplinary action
to be taken against the store manager whose behaviour had affected her health and
mental wellbeing. The names of various members of staff were given to the regional
HR manager to speak to. KCY further advised that there had been no duty of care or
follow up by the regional HR manager after concerns were raised with her in 2022.
KCY’s complaint investigated
[23] The formal investigation would be undertaken internally by XSH’ Head of HR
and its HR Manager Operations. Efforts to obtain a formal written statement from
KCY were not possible owing to her being on a period of sick leave from 21 to 27
September. In the circumstances, the regional HR manager drafted KCY’s statement
having regard to her complaint email of 11 September and the regional HR manager’s
file note of their second meeting on 13 September.
[24] The regional HR manager emailed the draft statement to KCY for her to make
any changes which she did on 5 October. During this time, the regional HR manager
was contacted by a mediator from the Human Rights Commission (HRC) who
advised that the applicant had lodged a complaint with it of discrimination on the
grounds of ethnicity or national origin. While proceedings in the HRC did not
progress to mediation, the involvement of the mediator proved useful as an
intermediary at times between the parties while XSH investigated the complaint.
[25] XSH’s draft report was completed by 13 October and it proposed four
recommendations including that the store manager be reminded of her status as store
manager and that her interest in the Russia/Ukraine conflict and any other like topics
were kept outside of work. It was also recommended that the assistance of the HRC
be sought to mediate a way forward between the parties.
[26] On 17 October, KCY was invited to a meeting with the store Regional
Manager and the HR Manager of Operations who read the draft report aloud and

provided her with a hardcopy. Although initially given two days to respond to the
draft report, this was twice extended by the respondent. When no response was
received, the store Regional Manager emailed a reminder that if nothing further was
provided by 3 November, the draft report would be finalised and the investigation
would be closed.
[27] On 22 November, KCY alleges that the store manager subjected her to an
uncomfortable and hostile environment and made her feel alienated from the rest of
the staff. Later that evening, she texted the store manager messages that on its face
were threatening: “Try ur best/ I had enough. U try to explain how I’m so dumb and
don’t see 100% :) I have so much on u :) and your faves :) Bring it on show up at
work and everything goes public” “I’m officially raising personal grievances against
you.”
[28] In explanation for the text messages, the applicant says that she had been
drinking wine that evening and stated that she regretted sending them. Upon
receiving her text messages, the store manager conveyed her concerns to the store
Regional Manager who agreed to be at the store the following morning before KCY
was expected to arrive. However, on that day it appears she had a panic attack in the
office which was witnessed by the regional HR manager and the store Regional
Manager. The applicant then went on a period of sick and pre-arranged annual leave
although the parties are in dispute as to when she was expected to return to work.
[29] On 27 November, the HRC mediator emailed the Head of HR that he had
received an email from KCY stating that she had been having a difficult time because
of a lot of tragic news about people she knew in Russia. She mentioned that she had
not lodged a personal grievance about that and wanted the mediator to let the Head of
HR know that she still wanted to provide feedback to her the report, which was
eventually provided on 12 December 2023.
[30] On 14 December, the Head of HR and the HR Manager Operations met with
KCY at one of its other flagship stores and suggested that she transfer there but she
declined the offer. On 18 December, the final report was completed and a copy
provided to KCY. The recommendations remained unchanged and the final report
stated that KCY had not raised a complaint of bullying with HR in November 2022.

[31] When the store Regional Manager learnt that KCY had declined to move to
the flagship store, he enabled her to transfer to a different local store closer to where
she lived. His intention in doing so was to reduce the tension between KCY and her
store manager while mediation was being arranged. The applicant commenced
working at the alternative local store on 20 December 2023.
Serious misconduct
[32] On 29 December, KCY attended her home store in which she originally
worked to purchase items on staff discount during non-working hours. As part of two
in-store purchases she made at that time, she collected two expired Gifts with
Purchase (GWP) namely an orange Elizabeth Arden bag and an Issy Miyake Bamboo
Glass Water bottle. Although the promotion periods for these GWPs had expired,
XSH maintains that KCY did not qualify for them because she did not have the
requisite authorisation from management. During that same visit, KCY provided a
member of staff with a piece of paper that had a code to a secure and restricted back-
office area which the respondent says the staff member was not authorised to enter.
[33] On 31 January 2024, XSH wrote to KCY inviting her to a disciplinary meeting
and alleging that she had breached the company’s GWP Guidelines and its Work
Rules around confidential information.
[34] The respondent referred the matter to another store manager to investigate
together with the HR Manager Operations. The respondent’s process afforded the
applicant the opportunity to respond to its preliminary findings of serious misconduct
and its subsequent proposed decision that she be summarily dismissed.
[35] By letter dated 20 May 2024, XSH dismissed KCY summarily for serious
misconduct.
Assessment
[36] The test of justification at s 103A of the Act requires the Authority to assess on
an objective basis whether an employer’s dismissal or action was what a fair and
reasonable employer could have done in all the circumstances at the time the dismissal
or action occurred. As part of this process, the Authority must consider the four

procedural fairness factors set out in s 103A(3) of the Act which are whether having
regard to the resources available to the employer: the allegations against the employee
were sufficiently investigated; whether the employer raised the concerns with the
employee before taking action; whether the employer gave the employee a reasonable
opportunity to respond to the concerns before taking action; and whether the employer
genuinely considered the employee’s explanations before dismissing or taking action
against the employee.
Whether the applicant was unjustifiably disadvantaged
Alleged bullying in the workplace
[37] KCY says that she was unjustifiably disadvantaged with her employment by
her employer’s failure to provide her with a safe working environment. It was
submitted that KCY’s email to the regional HR manager on 22 November 2022 was
her putting XSH on notice of “bullying” by the store manager. Although it is not in
dispute that KCY and the regional HR manager met for the first time on 29 November
to discuss her concerns, what was to happen after that meeting is the subject of
contention.
[38] No contemporaneous file note was taken by either party of this meeting and
although the regional HR manager eventually made one, this was created
approximately on 21 September 2023, some nine to ten months later. This is a
significant period for anyone to recall events with accuracy. In contrast, the applicant
who was allegedly being bullied by her store manager, will have remembered that
meeting vividly because it was an important meeting for her which she had arranged
on her own.
[39] I find that XSH was put on notice as early as late November 2022 that the
applicant was concerned that she was being bullied by the store manager; a tier 3
member of staff to whom KCY reported. Although it is noted that the regional HR
manager sent the applicant a follow-up text on 7 December to ‘touch base’ with her, a
fair and reasonable employer could still have followed up on the applicant just to
document the fact that nothing further from HR was required. By failing to do so,
XSH leaves itself open to the claim that it had failed to act.

[40] In the absence of a contemporaneously made file note of the 29 November
2022 meeting, and finding that matters discussed there would have resonated and
stuck with the applicant, I prefer KCY’s version of events as to what was to occur
next, which was HR to action her complaint which included the potential for
mediation to occur between the applicant and the store manager. The regional HR
manager’s failure to follow up with KCY after she did not respond to her 7 December
text resulted in the applicant experiencing further bullying by the store manager that
culminated in her having a significant panic attack at work on 6 September 2023.
[41] This claim of unjustified disadvantage has been established and gives rise to
remedies under s 123(1)(c)(i) of the Act for hurt and humiliation. KCY seeks an
award of $20,000 which falls in the mid-range of loss. Compensation is for the
effects on the employee of the grievance, and is not intended to be a penalty imposed
on the employer to indicate the Authority’s disapproval of the employer’s conduct.5
[42] According to a medical certificate from a GP (21 August 2025), the applicant
was previously of good health for the majority of her time she has been a patient of
the practice since 2005. According to the GP, the applicant was seen in September
2022 with respect to mental health concerns due to work stressors. She was not
started on any medications at that time but was supported by a mental health support
worker. However, in August 2023, KCY saw her GP who expressed great concern
about her stress which had worsened to such an extent that KCY needed to be started
on antidepressant medication.
[43] At the investigation meeting, KCY clarified that she had stopped taking
antidepressant medication in November 2024 and had received free counselling
sessions with Fresh Minds. The medical certificate indicates that the effects of the
grievance on the applicant are serious, but even so, there is no medical evidence
verifying KCY’s mental health from December 2022 to May 2023. This gap in the
chronology indicates that the store manager’s behaviour had abated for a time.
Although an award of $20,000 for hurt and humiliation is sought, I find an award of
$10,000 to be within range.
5 Paykel Ltd v Ahlfeld [1993] 1 ERNZ 334.

[44] As I have awarded this remedy to KCY, I must consider whether she has
contributed to the situation that has given rise to her personal grievance.6 It has been
suggested that she could have approached the regional HR manager or the store
Regional Manager when they visited the store in the aftermath of the Auckland
Anniversary floods in late January/early February 2023. However, there would have
been no need for the applicant to have done so as the store manager’s behaviour appears
to have abated at that time following the applicant’s one-on-one conversation with her
in December 2022.
[45] Neither can the award be reduced as a result of KCY’s failure to respond to the
regional HR manager’s text message of 7 December because the complaint against the
store manager had already been raised by then. Because it has not been demonstrated
that KCY has contributed to this disadvantage claim, a reduction in remedies is not
warranted under s 124 of the Act.
Whether a penalty under s 134(1) of the Act ought to be imposed
[46] KCY seeks a penalty under s 134 of the Act which states that every party to an
employment agreement who breaches that agreement is liable to a penalty. Both the
statutory considerations set out in s 133A and the additional considerations from the
relevant case law need to be collectively considered here. I find the regional HR
manager’s failure to take further steps in relation to her unanswered text to the applicant
was an oversight and not deliberate. It is not that kind of behaviour that ought to be
marked by a penalty which is declined.
Whether XSH’s investigation of KCY’s complaint was procedurally fair
[47] The applicant takes issue with her employer’s investigation of her complaint
because it did not interview her, failed to appoint a sufficiently independent
investigator, and did not ensure that interviewees were not influenced by the store
manager.
[48] The internal investigation of the applicant’s complaint against the store
manager was undertaken by the Head of HR and the HR Manager Operations and this
demonstrates that the respondent did take the complaint seriously. Although the
6 The Act, s 124.

applicant was not interviewed for the purposes of her written complaint statement, she
was given the opportunity to make any changes to that document which was compiled
for her having regard to KCY’s 11 September 2023 email to the regional HR manager
as well as the regional HR manager’s notes of their second meeting.
[49] As to whether a sufficiently independent investigator ought to have been
appointed, the store manager was a person who had worked for a significant period of
time and has recently retired. While the store manager would have been known to the
Head of HR and HR Manager Operations, more evidence is required before an
adverse finding of bias or partiality can reasonably be made.
[50] At the investigation meeting, KCY adduced an email from an interviewee
whom the store manager had escorted to the interview meeting room. However, no
weight can be given to the email because the interviewee was not made available for
cross-examination.
[51] For completeness, I note three other concerns KCY has raised with the
investigation. First, the regional HR manager made a file note of her and the store
Regional Manager’s meeting on 14 September 2023 with the store manager.7 That
file note was never disclosed to the applicant but even so, it has not been shown that
this has prejudiced the investigation. During the course of the investigation, the store
manager made two written statements to the Head of HR and HR Manager Operations
(11 October and 12 October 2023) that were disclosed to the applicant and which
reiterate various aspects of the undisclosed file note in any event.
[52] Second, the regional HR manager had emailed the Head of HR on
20 September 2023 that she had spoken to two interviewees who were confident that
there was no bullying by the store manager. On its face, the email suggests that the
regional HR manager was trying to influence the course of the investigation.
However, as she was not part of the investigation team, it is difficult to fathom how
that would be possible.
7 Common bundle, n 4, at p 078.

[53] Third, as part of the investigation, several interviewees appear to have been
spoken to by the Head of HR and HR Manager Operations before the applicant’s
formal written statement was received. While this was so, the investigators knew
what to ask these individuals as it had KCY’s emailed complaint of 11 September
2023 before them.
[54] I find no procedural unfairness with the investigation and while KCY
disagrees with the findings made, this does not demonstrate that the investigation
breached the principles of fairness and natural justice. This claim of unjustified
disadvantage has not been made out and is declined.
Whether KCY was unlawfully suspended
[55] The applicant contends that on 30 November 2023 she was sent home mid-
shift by the regional HR manager without proper explanation, prior consultation or
with her agreement. KCY says that she wanted to be at work but was excluded from
doing so.
[56] It is necessary to contextualise matters here. When the applicant attended
work on 30 November, she had on the evening of 22 November, and while
disinhibited by an unknown quantity of wine, sent a series of concerning text
messages to the store manager. The text messages were such that the store manager
contacted the store Regional Manager to let him know that she felt unsafe. Having
attended work the following morning on 23 November, KCY appears to have had
another panic attack that was witnessed by both the store Regional Manager and the
regional HR manager.
[57] As to what happened next, I prefer the evidence of the regional HR manager
who on this occasion did make a contemporaneous file note that same morning.
Among other things, the file note records:
[KCY] said she has been ok lately she just had a moment that’s why she
lashed out at [the store manager] via text – she is really sorry its
inappropriate she said. KCY said she can’t believe this is happening to her,
she can’t catch a break. We talked about her having a holiday … We then
arranged with [the store manager] for KCY to have 1 week off from Tuesday
28th November – 5th December.

[58] Given how emotionally upset the applicant was at the time, I prefer the
regional HR manager’s evidence who made a contemporaneous file note to document
what was discussed that morning. The file note demonstrates that the applicant was
not unjustifiably disadvantaged because she had been suspended from work from
30 November to 5 December. She was in fact on agreed leave during this period.
[59] As to KCY’s contention that she was further suspended as a result of the store
Regional Manager emailing her on 4 December to request a medical certificate
showing that she was well enough to return to work on the 5th, the request for a
medical certificate was what a fair and reasonable employer could have done in all the
circumstances. Only 11 days earlier, the applicant had sent a series of concerning text
messages to the store manager and suffered a panic attack at work. As she been away
on leave, it was prudent of the store Regional Manager to inquire whether KCY was
well enough to return to work and if so, in what capacity.
[60] KCY says at [83] in her first written statement to the Authority (2 September
2025) that she did not see the store Regional Manager’s email of 4 December until
7 December. She then obtained a letter from her GP (11 December 2023) who
expressed confidence in her stability and capability to return to work. However, the
GP noted that the applicant had confided in her that her current work environment
was a “toxic work environment.”
[61] Reference in the medical certificate of a toxic work environment put the
respondent in an unenviable position because allowing her return to work could leave
it vulnerable to further criticism that it had failed to keep her safe even if it denied the
allegation. While the store Regional Manager was correct to be concerned, he could
have telephoned the applicant about this new concern and offered her the opportunity
to provide further comment before placing her on paid special leave for a further
seven days from 12 to 19 December.
[62] The lack of consultation gives rise to an unlawful suspension especially as
KCY had provided, as requested, a medical certificate which showed that she was fit
to return to work. Placing the applicant on special leave was procedurally unjustified
and fails the test of justification at s 103A of the Act.

[63] KCY is entitled to remedies for this unjustified disadvantage claim. The effect
of not being able to return to work made the applicant feel that she was being targeted.
Even so, the suspension grievance did not result in the same degree of harm and this
must be reflected in the compensation to be awarded for hurt and humiliation.
Compensation at the lower level of loss of $3,000 is appropriate. As the applicant has
not contributed to this grievance no reduction is made under s 124 of the Act.
Whether KCY was unilaterally transferred to another store
[64] KCY submits that she was unilaterally transferred from her home store to an
alternative local store. XSH says that the applicant had previously declined a job
opportunity for personal reasons at one of its flagship stores and that the subsequent
transfer to the alternative local store was a temporary measure until mediation
between KCY and the store manager could be arranged. However, there is a paucity
of evidence of proper consultation regarding the transfer to the alternative local store.
[65] The applicant’s individual employment agreement with XSH relevantly states:
You must be prepared to be flexible to meet the needs of the business … The
company reserves the right, at any time during your tenure, to alter hours or
days of work, or to relocate you … We will consult as widely as possible …
[66] While I accept the transfer to the alternative local store was intended to be
temporary, no date for mediation was scheduled and being a voluntary process, when
that could realistically take place if at all remains unclear on the evidence.
[67] Regarding the lack of consultation about the transfer to the local alternative
store, the store Regional Manager’s letter of 19 December 2023 to the applicant was
essentially a fait accompli, leaving KCY with no opportunity to comment:
Please report to the [alternative local store] tomorrow morning at 9 am,
where I will meet with you to introduce you to the team and ensure you are
orientated appropriately. If you fail to attend work at [the alternative local
store], we will consider that you are on unpaid leave and will take the
necessary steps to address this in your January pay.
[68] The respondent’s action in transferring the applicant in the way that it did and
requiring her to work in a different workplace the very next day (20 December) falls
well short of the employer’s obligation under s 103A(3)(c) of the Act. The section

requires the employer to give their employee a reasonable opportunity to respond to
the employer’s concern before taking action against the employee.
[69] This gives rise to a separate award of compensation under s 123(1)(c)(i) of the
Act for hurt and humiliation. KCY would have accepted the transfer to the alternative
local store had she been consulted but she was not and although XSH denies
threatening the applicant with unpaid leave if she rejected the transfer, the reality was
that if she wanted to be paid, she needed to accept the transfer.
[70] The compensation award for this disadvantage falls in the range of low-to-mid
loss of $10,000. However, the transfer would not have come about but for the
applicant’s distressing text messages to the store manager. I find that KCY has
contributed to this unjustified disadvantage grievance in a significant way warranting
an 70 percent reduction under s 124 of the Act. This results in a reduced
compensation award in the amount of $3,000 for this personal grievance.
Whether KCY was unjustifiably dismissed
[71] The applicant’s employment ended for serious misconduct for an alleged
breach of the respondent’s Gift with Purchase (GWP) Guidelines (the Guidelines) and
disclosing to a work colleague the door code to a restricted area.
[72] Generally serious misconduct is behaviour by an employee that fundamentally
breaches the trust and confidence essential to the employment relationship rendering its
continuation untenable. It is more than mere inadvertence, oversight or negligence and
the Court of Appeal has said that summary dismissal usually involves “conduct that
deeply impairs or is destructive of that basic confidence or trust that is an essential of
the employment relationship.”8
[73] What serious misconduct may look like from one case to the next will inevitably
vary because the conduct or breach in question and its circumstances, the particular
contractual obligations on the employee arising from the employment relationship, the
nature of the work place or industry, and aspects of the case that may engage the public
interest, are not always the same and it is these subtle distinctions that make the
8 Northern Distribution Union v BP Oil New Zealand Ltd [1992] 3 CRNZ 483.

difference between a breach that amounts to serious misconduct or something more
benign.
[74] The relevant case law states that the assessment of serious misconduct involves
a two-step approach which involves as a first step, considering whether the conduct in
question is capable of amounting to serious misconduct; if it is, then the second step is
to consider whether dismissal is warranted in all the circumstances.9
[75] At the time of the dismissal, the applicant was employed in the role of beauty
sales manager at one of the respondent’s retail stores. It was a role that she had held
from 1 May 2022 until she was summarily dismissed for serious misconduct on
20 May 2024. KCY’s individual employment agreement with XSH included the
following terms and conditions:
Terms of Employment
… You must abide by all rules, procedures and policies currently in force (or
as modified from time to time by the company) … and it shall be your
responsibility to familiarise yourself with such rules, policies and procedures.
Confidentiality
… Disclosure of other commercially sensitive and or customer information
will be viewed as a breach of confidentiality and may lead to disciplinary
action, and in addition may be a breach of the Privacy Act.
[76] Appendix 1 to the individual employment agreement contained the
respondent’s Work Rules and Disciplinary Procedures which sets out a non-
exhaustive list of what could constitute serious misconduct:
1. Property
Unauthorised possession, unauthorised removal or unauthorised wilful
movement of Company property or the property of other persons.
…
6. Company Procedures
Failure to follow the correct procedure for the operation of company systems.
7. Confidential Information
Confidential information gained during the course of employment must not
be released to persons who could materially affect [XSH’s] interests.
9 Auckland Provincial District Local Authorities Officers IUOW v Northland Area Health Board
[1991] 2 ERNZ 215 (LC) at 222; Emmanuel v Waikato District Health Board [2019] NZEmpC 81 at
[59]; Morris v Fire and Emergency New Zealand [2025] NZERA 612 at [103].

[77] On 29 December 2023, KCY purchased at her home store in which she
originally worked before being transferred to work at the alternative local store the
following products:
(i) Elizabeth Arden Retinol Ceramide Capsules for $97 and
obtained an Elizabeth Arden GWP namely an orange bag
although the applicant was after a yellow bag which she knew to
be in store.
(ii) Good Girl Blush 3-piece Christmas 23 set for $284 and obtained
a different brand GWP namely an Issy Miyake Bamboo glass
water bottle.
Both of the above GWPs were ‘expired’ meaning that their respective promotion
periods had ended.
[78] Before attending her home store, KCY had checked at the alternative local
store whether the Elizabeth Arden GWP yellow bag was available there, which stock
records indicated that it was. Visiting her home store, the applicant inquired about the
yellow bag which she knew to be available. However, the beauty counter staff at the
home store had decided in advance not to give the yellow bag to the applicant but
rather keep it for their valued clients. The advice they gave to KCY was that the
GWP yellow bag was not available.
[79] KCY was not aware of the deception and in the course of trying to find the
yellow bag provided a beauty counter staff member the door code to a restricted office
area to see if the GWP yellow bag was held there. Feeling uncomfortable that she
could get into trouble because she had been given the code to the office, the beauty
counter staff member did not go into the office but feigned doing so and reported to
KCY that she could not find the yellow bag. The applicant left the store with the
GWP orange bag instead.
GWP Guidelines
[80] The respondent’s policies include the Guidelines which states:

In some instances, once a promotion is over, the GWPs are required to be
returned to the vendor. Where [XSH] can keep the GWP, it is expected that
the salesperson will continue to give away the GWP as long as the customer
is purchasing the product(s) of the same brand as the GWP and of a value
equal to or exceeding $20.
Although the GWP is not a direct cost to [XSH], it is a cost to the supplier.
Therefore, the relationship with our supplier must be protected by ensuring
that we use the GWP for the purpose that was intended for, that is, to drive
and increase sales of the brand.
…
Any old GWP’s provided to staff with Purchase, must be authorised by
Management specifically the Store Manager, ASMO, ASMS and BSM.
[81] KCY contends that she was not aware of the Guidelines which the respondent
rejects as the Guidelines are part of the Store Operations Manual which the
applicant’s employment agreement required to be familiar with. Although KCY
never signed an acknowledgement of the Guidelines and, while there is a lack of
evidence that a training module that staff are required to undertake covers the
Guidelines, being a tier 2 manager to whom people working on the floor reported,
KCY can reasonably be expected to be across the Guidelines.
[82] That said, prima facie, under the Guidelines, and having spent over $20 for
her Elizabeth Arden Retinol Ceramide Capsules, KCY did qualify for a GWP. The
respondent’s final decision letter (20 May 2024) in which it terminated KCY for
serious misconduct was not correct on this point. It was incorrect that the applicant
did not qualify for a GWP (the Elizabeth Arden orange bag) but any old GWP still
needed to be authorised by management.
[83] As for KCY’s second purchase of a Good Girl Blush 3-piece set, although this
was a significant purchase at $284, technically the Guidelines required the GWP to be
of the same brand which Issy Miyake is not. Despite this, various customer receipts
were provided which show that the counter beauty manager who had served KCY on
29 December had processed similar transactions for other customers who received
GWP that were not of the same brand. As there is evidence of the Guidelines not
being adhered to by staff, the fact that KCY received GWP of a different brand could
not if itself be determinative.

[84] In applying the test of justification at s 103A of the Act, there are four key
factors for consideration as noted above at [36]. Of those factors and for the reasons
that follow, I find that the respondent has not genuinely considered the applicant’s
explanation in relation to her alleged breach of the Guidelines.
[85] On 9 January 2023, the Head of HR emailed the regional HR manager the
following after learning of the allegations:10
We need to investigate this very carefully to ensure that what [KCY] is
asking isn’t common practice in this store? The rules are very clear but it
needs to be thoroughly covered off before we proceed further.
[86] Although this email was sent very early in the company’s disciplinary process
and well before any views on the merits were formed, the possibility of the home
store having developed its own common practice was never properly investigated
because it was considered irrelevant. The issue matters because KCY had tried to
obtain the transactions records of the beauty counter manager that had served her to
show that there was a common practice of staff at the home store not having
management authorise the issuing of expired GWPs to staff.
[87] While the store manager of another XSH store was brought in to be an
independent decision maker, when cross-examined he said that the request for the
beauty counter manager’s transactions was a “side issue”, that he was not looking at
whether there was a common practice, that the request was irrelevant, and that what
he was dealing with was a beauty sales manager (KCY) who should have known
better.
[88] The HR Manager Operations who assisted the decision maker gave similar
responses when asked about the applicant’s request for the counter beauty manager’s
transactions stating that if a breach occurred, a breach occurred and that he did not see
the relevance in disclosing this information to the applicant.
[89] It is difficult to comprehend how an experienced store manager and the HR
Manager Operations could both not see the relevance of the counter beauty manager’s
transactions.
10 Supplementary bundle, 16 February 2026, SB43.

[90] The information was relevant because if there was evidence of a common
practice of staff at the home store not complying with Guidelines, this would
contextualise KCY’s breach and become a mitigating factor requiring consideration
by the decision maker.
[91] As for the provision of the door code to another member of staff at the beauty
counter, the decision maker and the HR Manager Operations investigation did not
sufficiently look into why various staff members of the beauty counter team had
deliberately misled KCY about the yellow bag. Had that not happened, the passing of
the door code by the applicant would most likely not have happened. That said, the
provision of the code to the staff member in this manner was unusual and probably
not standard protocol, but this complaint of itself would not have been enough to
constitute serious misconduct when all the circumstances are fairly and reasonably
taken into account.
[92] On balance, a fair and reasonable employer could not have summarily
dismissed the applicant for serious misconduct on these facts. I find that KCY was
unjustifiably dismissed and that she is entitled to remedies.
Compensation for unjustified dismissal
[93] KCY says in her first written witness statement to the Authority that
throughout her employment she had no prior record of misconduct, that her
performance reviews were consistently positive, that her dismissal was abrupt and
devastating, and that as a single mother she was plunged into severe financial stress.
KCY further says that she was forced to urgently seek alternative housing and mental
health support to cope with the trauma, embarrassment, and mistreatment that she
experienced.
[94] I find that the effects of KCY’s dismissal personal grievance falls in the mid-
to-high range of loss of $30,000. As for contribution, it was submitted that the
confusion on 29 December 2023 arose due to the deceptive actions of other staff who
misled the applicant about whether the yellow bag GWP was available. While I agree
with counsel about the deception, of the range of responses the applicant could have
reasonably chosen, the giving of the passcode was misconceived and has partially

contributed to her dismissal grievance. A reduction of 20 percent to the compensation
award under s 124 of the Act is warranted.
Lost wages
[95] As for reimbursement of lost remuneration under s 128 of the Act, the earliest
evidence of KCY having applied for alternative employment was from November
2024 some six months after the dismissal. Although it remains unclear why KCY has
not applied for work sooner than this, the question that needs to be asked is not what
steps she should have taken to mitigate her loss but what might reasonably have been
expected of her in the particular circumstances.11 It would have been a tumultuous
period for the applicant both financially and mentally and the challenges these present
in being able to look for work must be taken into consideration. Rather than disentitle
KCY of this remedy altogether, I adopt the default position of three months’ lost
remuneration under s 128 of the Act minus 20 percent for contribution under s 124.
Whether annual leave should be reimbursed
[96] The applicant seeks reimbursement of annual leave in the amount of 88 hours.
The common bundle includes a point-in-time payroll report for KCY which is
incorrect. For the period 28-29 November 2023, KCY was at work and not on annual
leave. Although she says she was permitted to return to work on 30 November, I have
found that she agreed to return on 5 December and should still have been on annual
leave that day.
[97] For the period of 5 to 12 December 2023 which is recorded as being ‘annual
leave’, the applicant was in fact on paid special leave and not ‘annual leave taken’.
The applicant is entitled to reimbursement of annual leave for these periods as well.
Whether to award general damages
[98] The applicant seeks general damages for non-economic loss but I have
declined to do so for the remedies she has been awarded in the Authority will
subsume any other losses that she may have suffered.
11 Maddigan v Director-General of Conservation [2019] NZEmpC 190 at [62].

Conclusion
[99] For the reasons given above, I have found that KCY was unjustifiably
disadvantaged in her employment but not all of her disadvantage claims have been
successful. I have also found that she was unjustifiably dismissed from her
employment but that she has also contributed to that personal grievance.
Summary of Orders
[100] XSH is ordered to pay KCY by Monday 31 August 2026 the following sums:
(i) Compensation of $10,000 under s 123(1)(c)(i) of the Act for
the unjustified disadvantage arising from HR’s failure to
follow up with the applicant concerning her bullying complaint
in November 2022.
(ii) Compensation of $3,000 under s 123(1)(c)(i) of the Act for the
unjustified disadvantage from the applicant not being properly
consulted that saw her being placed on paid special leave from
12-19 December 2023.
(iii) Compensation of $3,000 under s 123(1)(c)(i) and s 124 of the
Act for the unjustified disadvantage relating to being
transferred to another store.
(iv) Compensation of $24,000 under s 123(1)(c)(i) and s 124 of the
Act for unjustified dismissal.
(v) Reimbursement of three months’ lost remuneration less
20 percent under s 128 and s 124 of the Act.
(vi) Reimbursement of annual leave for 28, 29 November and 5-12
December 2023.
